title: Only 5% Of Adults Can Ace This Idiom Quiz
summary: Hidden meanings, emoji clues, missing words and almost-right expressions get trickier across 10 fast rounds.

landing.intro: Think you know what people really mean? Decode hidden meanings, missing words and almost-right expressions before they catch you out.

about.body:
This worldwide-English idiom quiz turns familiar expressions into ten increasingly tricky rounds of meanings, missing words, emoji clues, dialogue and almost-right phrases. It is designed to test practical language comprehension—the kind used in conversation, media, education and everyday communication—without relying on obscure origins or local slang.

Each question focuses on one widely understood expression and asks you to interpret, complete or use it precisely. Correct answers stay hidden until the end, so every response reflects your own sense of context, tone and figurative meaning rather than feedback from an earlier round.

Your final percentage is an entertainment score based only on these sixty questions. The complete review explains every expression, making the challenge useful for fluent speakers, language learners and anyone who enjoys sharpening communication skills.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Answer six questions in each round by choosing the meaning, word or expression best supported by the visible clue.
Read carefully: emoji, dialogue, tone and one almost-right word can completely change the answer.
Complete all ten rounds to reveal your Idiom Score, strongest language skill and full answer review.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This quiz is not a formal English-language assessment or qualification.

profiles.title: The Phrase Master
profiles.copy: You read figurative language with remarkable precision, even when the wording, tone and context tried to pull you off course. Familiar phrases and subtle intentions clicked into place almost instantly.

profiles.title: The Natural Wordsmith
profiles.copy: You have an excellent feel for what expressions really mean and when they belong. Only a few of the challenge’s finer wording traps managed to catch you out.

profiles.title: The Idiom Insider
profiles.copy: You decoded most hidden meanings and handled a broad mix of phrases with confidence. A handful of precise words or less obvious contexts kept the test interesting.

profiles.title: The Context Catcher
profiles.copy: You often found the intended meaning by reading the situation rather than taking every word literally. Your strongest round shows which kind of language clue works best for you.

profiles.title: The Phrase Explorer
profiles.copy: You recognised a solid share of the expressions and kept finding meaning when the format changed. The answer review will turn the phrases that slipped past into useful new clues.

profiles.title: The Literal Wildcard
profiles.copy: Some of the figurative language stayed determinedly mysterious, but your answers still uncovered moments of sharp context reading. Every explanation is a chance to add another expression to your conversational toolkit.

score.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This quiz is not a formal English-language assessment or qualification.

questions.question: What does “break the ice” mean?
answers: Make people feel comfortable enough to start talking
Make a difficult task look easy
questions.explanation: “Break the ice” means easing initial tension so conversation can begin more comfortably.

questions.question: Complete the expression: “a piece of ___”
questions.explanation: “A piece of cake” describes something that is very easy to do.

questions.question: Which person is “under the weather”?
answers: Kai is caught outside in heavy rain
Noah feels unwell and stays home to rest
questions.explanation: Someone who is “under the weather” feels slightly ill; Noah’s need to rest is the supporting clue.

questions.question: “Come on—spill the beans!” What does the speaker want?
questions.explanation: “Spill the beans” is an informal request to reveal secret or previously hidden information.

questions.question: Which weather matches “raining cats and dogs”?
questions.explanation: “Raining cats and dogs” means raining extremely heavily; the downpour icon carries the clue.

questions.question: Which expression correctly means “identify the exact point”?
answers: Hit the hammer on the nail
Hit the nail on the head
Put the nail in the point
Strike the point with a hammer
questions.explanation: The canonical expression is “hit the nail on the head,” meaning to say or identify exactly what is right.

questions.question: A team is “on the same page.” What is true?
questions.explanation: Being “on the same page” means sharing an understanding or agreeing about what should happen.

questions.question: Complete: “once in a blue ___”

visual.ariaLabel: Once in, a blue, missing word

questions.explanation: “Once in a blue moon” means very rarely.

questions.question: Complete: “cost an arm and a ___”
questions.explanation: The expression “cost an arm and a leg” describes something that is extremely expensive.

questions.question: Complete: “burn the midnight ___”
questions.explanation: To “burn the midnight oil” is to work or study late into the night.

questions.question: Complete: “let the cat out of the ___”
questions.explanation: To “let the cat out of the bag” is to reveal a secret, often accidentally.

questions.question: Which expression means to tease someone playfully?
questions.explanation: To “pull someone’s leg” means to joke with or playfully deceive them.

questions.question: What does 🚶 + 🥚 suggest?
answers: Acting very carefully to avoid upsetting someone
questions.explanation: “Walking on eggshells” means behaving very carefully because a person or situation is sensitive.

questions.question: “Please keep an eye on my bag.” What should you do?
questions.explanation: To “keep an eye on” something means to watch or monitor it for a time.

questions.question: Which outcome fits 🗯️ + ⛽ + 🔥?
questions.explanation: To “add fuel to the fire” is to make an already difficult or angry situation worse.

questions.question: Which image best represents feeling out of place?
questions.explanation: A “fish out of water” is someone uncomfortable because they are in an unfamiliar setting.

questions.question: Everyone ignores 🐘 during a tense meeting. What is it?
answers: An obvious problem nobody wants to discuss
questions.explanation: The “elephant in the room” is an obvious, important issue that people avoid acknowledging.

questions.question: Which clue shows two people agreeing?
questions.explanation: People who “see eye to eye” agree; the joined-eye clue represents shared understanding.

questions.question: Which situation is “back to square one”?
answers: A team finishes ahead of schedule
A plan needs one tiny adjustment
A new member joins halfway through
The only prototype fails and the team must restart
questions.explanation: “Back to square one” means returning to the beginning after progress or a plan has failed.

questions.question: After hours of work, everyone is tired. What fits best?
questions.explanation: To “call it a day” is to stop working on something for the rest of that period.

questions.question: Who “goes the extra mile”?
answers: Asha does only the minimum requested
Ben finishes the task and adds genuinely useful help
Dara leaves before the work begins
questions.explanation: To “go the extra mile” is to make more effort than is expected; Ben adds helpful work beyond the requirement.

questions.question: The meeting is silent. What would “get the ball rolling”?
questions.explanation: To “get the ball rolling” is to start an activity or process; the first useful question begins the discussion.

questions.question: Someone keeps joking while everyone else is visibly upset. What did they fail to do?
questions.explanation: To “read the room” is to notice the mood and adapt appropriately; the visible upset is the key clue.

questions.question: Which phrase means refusing to choose between two sides?
questions.explanation: To “sit on the fence” is to avoid committing to either side of a decision or argument.

questions.question: A cancelled trip led Mira to a better opportunity. What was the cancellation?
questions.explanation: A “blessing in disguise” seems bad at first but later produces a good result.

questions.question: “The event moved online, but more people could attend.” What is the extra reach?
questions.explanation: A “silver lining” is the positive aspect of an otherwise difficult situation.

questions.question: A small visible issue hints at a much larger hidden problem. Which phrase fits?

visual.ariaLabel: Small visible part above a large hidden part

questions.explanation: The “tip of the iceberg” is the small visible part of something much larger that remains hidden.

questions.question: “They supported each other in easy years and difficult ones.” What does this describe?
answers: A relationship based only on success
questions.explanation: Staying with someone “through thick and thin” means remaining loyal in both good and bad times.

questions.question: The venue and date are still undecided. The plan is…
questions.explanation: Something “up in the air” is uncertain or not yet decided; both key details remain unsettled.

questions.question: “Thanks, but horror films are not my cup of tea.” What is the speaker saying?
answers: They do not personally enjoy horror films
They have never seen a film
They think nobody should watch them
questions.explanation: “Not my cup of tea” politely says that something is not to one’s personal taste.

questions.question: Jo keeps discussing side details instead of answering. What is Jo doing?
questions.explanation: To “beat around the bush” is to avoid addressing the main point directly.

questions.question: A newcomer seems quiet but gives a brilliant presentation. Which reminder fits?
answers: Don’t judge a book by its cover
questions.explanation: “Don’t judge a book by its cover” warns against deciding what someone or something is like from appearance alone.

questions.question: “Just stay calm during the exam!” Why might someone reply, “Easier said than done”?
answers: The advice is simpler to give than to follow
The advice is technically impossible to hear
questions.explanation: “Easier said than done” means an action sounds simple but is difficult to carry out.

questions.question: A friend is struggling but making progress. Which message is encouraging?
questions.explanation: “Hang in there” encourages someone to persist through a difficult period.

questions.question: After a fair disagreement, Sam says, “No hard feelings.” What is the intent?
answers: To say there is no lasting resentment
questions.explanation: “No hard feelings” says the speaker holds no continuing anger or resentment.

questions.question: Which phrase means choosing a favourable explanation when proof is incomplete?
questions.explanation: Giving someone “the benefit of the doubt” means accepting the more favourable interpretation when certainty is unavailable.

questions.question: Registration closed yesterday. Ari has “missed the boat.” What happened?
answers: Ari arrived at the wrong building
Ari acted too late and lost the chance
questions.explanation: To “miss the boat” is to act too late and lose an opportunity.

questions.question: Complete the good-luck wish used before a performance: “break a ___”
questions.explanation: “Break a leg” is a traditional informal way to wish a performer good luck.

questions.question: Which clue shows someone daydreaming instead of concentrating?
questions.explanation: Someone with their “head in the clouds” is daydreaming or not paying attention to practical matters.

questions.question: Which expression correctly means pursuing the wrong person or explanation?
questions.explanation: “Barking up the wrong tree” means following a mistaken line of thought or blaming the wrong person.

questions.question: Which is the canonical expression for joining something because it is popular?
questions.explanation: To “jump on the bandwagon” is to join a popular activity, trend or opinion.

questions.question: Which expression says to handle a possible problem only if it happens?
answers: Build that bridge before we need it
Cross that bridge when we come to it
Close that bridge when we see it
questions.explanation: “Cross that bridge when we come to it” means dealing with a problem when it actually arises rather than worrying now.

questions.question: The next decision is yours. Which phrase fits?
answers: The ball is in your court
The choice has left the field
questions.explanation: “The ball is in your court” means it is now your responsibility to decide or act.

questions.question: Complete: “better late than ___”
questions.explanation: “Better late than never” says doing something late is preferable to not doing it at all.

questions.question: Which phrase encourages optimism?
questions.explanation: “Keep your chin up” encourages someone to stay positive during difficulty.

questions.question: Which reply shows strong doubt?
answers: I have already seen it happen
questions.explanation: “I wouldn’t hold my breath” shows the speaker doubts something will happen soon, if at all.

questions.question: Which clue means time passes quickly?
questions.explanation: “Time flies” means time seems to pass very quickly; the winged clock carries that visual idea.

questions.question: Which phrase asks for the main point?
questions.explanation: “Cut to the chase” means getting directly to the important point without unnecessary detail.

questions.question: Which expression is correct?
answers: Take the bull through the horns
Take the bull by the horns
Take the bull from the horns
Take the bull beneath the horns
questions.explanation: The fixed wording is “take the bull by the horns,” meaning to confront a difficult situation directly; “by” is the exact lexical clue.

questions.question: Which expression is correct?
questions.explanation: The canonical phrase is “the best of both worlds,” meaning enjoying the advantages of two different situations; “of” is required.

questions.question: Which phrase names the final irritation that ends someone’s patience?
questions.explanation: “The last straw” is the final problem in a series that makes a situation unbearable; “last” is the precise word.

questions.question: Which expression links two contrasting parts of one issue?
answers: Two faces of the same coin
Two sides from the same coin
Two sides of the same coin
Two sides beneath the same coin
questions.explanation: “Two sides of the same coin” describes closely connected aspects of one issue; “sides of” is the fixed wording.

questions.question: Which version correctly describes a past issue no longer worth arguing about?
questions.explanation: The canonical expression is “water under the bridge”; “under the” is the exact fixed wording for a past matter now accepted.

questions.question: Which expression correctly means to give up?
questions.explanation: “Throw in the towel” means admit defeat or stop trying; “in the” is the fixed lexical form.

questions.question: The target was 80%. After I reached it, the judge demanded 90%. What happened?
questions.context: The original condition was met, then the condition changed to make success harder.
answers: The judge offered a second chance
questions.explanation: To “move the goalposts” is to unfairly change the rules or requirements after progress has been made; both percentages show the shift.

questions.question: The office is unusually quiet just before a hectic launch. Complete the expression.
questions.context: Current mood: peaceful. Expected next: intense activity.
questions.explanation: “The calm before the storm” is a quiet period immediately before trouble or intense activity; the contrast and timing provide both clues.

questions.question: Investigators check every record and interview every witness. Which phrase fits?
questions.context: They search thoroughly and deliberately exclude no possible source.
questions.explanation: To “leave no stone unturned” is to search or investigate every possible avenue; both the records and witnesses show the thoroughness.

questions.question: Sales keep falling and every branch is reducing hours. What warning is becoming clear?
questions.context: Two visible trends point towards an unwelcome outcome before it is officially announced.
answers: The report is hard to read
The writing is on the wall
questions.explanation: “The writing is on the wall” means clear signs show that something bad is likely; falling sales and reduced hours are the two warning clues.

questions.question: One small question reveals five tangled problems. Which image-based phrase fits?
questions.context: A simple action creates a complicated set of new difficulties.

visual.ariaLabel: One question leads to many problems and more questions

questions.explanation: To “open a can of worms” is to create or uncover a complicated collection of problems; the one-to-many chain is the key clue.

questions.question: A single matching file is hidden among thousands of nearly identical ones. Which phrase fits?
questions.context: The target is tiny, the search area is huge and most items look alike.

visual.ariaLabel: One thin target hidden among many similar marks

questions.explanation: A “needle in a haystack” is something extremely difficult to find because it is hidden among many similar things; the tiny target and huge field supply both clues.
